title: Deploying Models to Kubernetes
summary: Learn how to deploy a containerized model API to a Kubernetes cluster using core objects: Pods, Deployments, and Services. This lesson covers writing manifests, exposing your API, applying probes and resource limits, and verifying rollouts with kubectl.
objectives: Explain the role of Pods, Deployments, and Services in running a model API on Kubernetes
Write and apply YAML manifests to deploy a containerized model API
Expose the model API internally and externally using Service types
Configure liveness/readiness probes and resource requests/limits for reliability
Verify, scale, and roll out updates to a deployment using kubectl

quiz.q: Which Kubernetes object should you create to run a stateless model API with self-healing and rolling updates?
quiz.why: A Deployment manages a ReplicaSet of identical Pods and provides scaling, self-healing, and rolling updates. You rarely create bare Pods directly.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of a Service in Kubernetes?
options: To provide a stable network endpoint that load-balances across matching Pods
quiz.why: Pods are ephemeral and get new IPs; a Service provides a stable virtual IP/DNS name and load-balances traffic to Pods matched by its label selector.

quiz.q: Which probe prevents traffic from reaching a Pod whose model weights are still loading?
quiz.why: The readiness probe signals when a Pod is ready to receive traffic. Until it passes, the Service won't route requests to that Pod.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid using the 'latest' image tag in production deployments?
options: It makes rollouts and rollbacks unpredictable
quiz.why: With 'latest' you can't reliably know which version is running, and rollbacks become unpredictable. Pin specific, immutable tags instead.

quiz.q: In a Service manifest, what do 'port' and 'targetPort' refer to respectively?
quiz.answer: port is the port clients use to reach the Service; targetPort is the port the container is listening on.
quiz.why: Clients connect to the Service on 'port', which forwards traffic to the Pod's 'targetPort' (the containerPort).

quiz.q: Which kubectl command reverts a Deployment to its previous version after a bad release?
quiz.why: kubectl rollout undo reverts the Deployment to the prior ReplicaSet revision, enabling a quick rollback without manually editing manifests.

resources.label: Configure Liveness, Readiness and Startup Probes

body_markdown:
## Why Kubernetes for Model Serving

Once your model API is containerized, you need a way to run it reliably, scale it, and recover from failures. Kubernetes (k8s) is the de-facto orchestrator for this. It schedules containers across a cluster, restarts crashed processes, balances traffic, and enables zero-downtime updates.

For an MLOps engineer, the key insight is that you describe the **desired state** in declarative manifests, and Kubernetes continuously reconciles the cluster to match that state.

## Core Objects

- **Pod**: the smallest deployable unit — one (or a few tightly-coupled) containers sharing network and storage. You rarely create Pods directly.
- **Deployment**: manages a set of identical Pods via a ReplicaSet. Handles scaling, rolling updates, and self-healing. This is what you use for a stateless model API.
- **Service**: a stable network endpoint (virtual IP + DNS name) that load-balances traffic across the Pods matched by a label selector. Pods are ephemeral and get new IPs; a Service gives you a fixed address.

## A Deployment Manifest

A Deployment wraps a Pod template. The `selector` must match the Pod `labels`. Always pin a specific image tag (avoid `latest` in production).

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: model-api
  labels:
    app: model-api
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: model-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: model-api
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: model-api
          image: registry.example.com/model-api:1.2.0
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: "250m"
              memory: "512Mi"
            limits:
              cpu: "1"
              memory: "1Gi"
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /ready
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 10
            periodSeconds: 5
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 20
            periodSeconds: 10
```

## Exposing the API with a Service

A Service selects Pods by label and routes traffic to them. Common types:

- **ClusterIP** (default): reachable only inside the cluster — good for internal microservices.
- **NodePort**: opens a port on every node — useful for quick testing.
- **LoadBalancer**: provisions an external load balancer (on cloud providers) — typical for public endpoints.

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: model-api
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: model-api
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
```

Here `port` is the Service port clients hit, and `targetPort` is the container port. For external HTTP traffic you typically front a ClusterIP Service with an **Ingress** controller.

## Probes and Resources Matter

- **Readiness probe**: tells Kubernetes when a Pod can receive traffic. Model APIs often need time to load weights — a readiness probe prevents requests hitting a not-yet-ready Pod.
- **Liveness probe**: restarts a Pod that has hung or deadlocked.
- **Resource requests** drive scheduling; **limits** cap usage. Models can be memory-hungry, so set realistic values to avoid OOM kills and noisy-neighbor problems.

## Applying and Verifying

```bash
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
kubectl apply -f service.yaml

kubectl get pods -l app=model-api
kubectl get deployment model-api
kubectl describe pod <pod-name>
kubectl logs <pod-name>

# Test locally without external exposure
kubectl port-forward svc/model-api 8080:80
```

## Scaling and Rolling Updates

```bash
# Scale
kubectl scale deployment model-api --replicas=5

# Update image (triggers a rolling update)
kubectl set image deployment/model-api model-api=registry.example.com/model-api:1.3.0
kubectl rollout status deployment/model-api

# Roll back if something breaks
kubectl rollout undo deployment/model-api
```

Deployments perform rolling updates by default, spinning up new Pods before terminating old ones, giving you zero-downtime releases when probes are configured correctly.

## Common Pitfalls

- Selector labels not matching Pod template labels → Deployment manages nothing.
- Using `latest` tag → unpredictable rollouts and broken rollbacks.
- No readiness probe → traffic sent to Pods still loading models.
- No resource requests → poor scheduling and OOM kills.

slides.title: Deploying Models to Kubernetes
slides.sub: Pods, Deployments & Services for your model API
slides.narration: Welcome. In this lesson we'll take a containerized model API and deploy it to a Kubernetes cluster. We'll cover the three core building blocks — Pods, Deployments, and Services — and walk through the manifests and commands you'll use day to day as an MLOps engineer.

slides.title: Why Kubernetes
bullets: Schedules containers across a cluster automatically
Self-heals by restarting failed Pods
Scales replicas up and down on demand
Enables zero-downtime rolling updates
You declare desired state; k8s reconciles it
slides.narration: Once your model is in a container, you need something to run it reliably in production. Kubernetes is the standard orchestrator. The mental model to hold onto is declarative: you describe the desired state in YAML, and Kubernetes continuously works to make the cluster match that state — restarting crashes, balancing traffic, and rolling out updates.

slides.title: The Three Core Objects
bullets: Pod: smallest unit, runs your container(s)
Deployment: manages identical Pods, handles scaling & updates
Service: stable network endpoint that load-balances to Pods
You manage Deployments, not Pods directly
Services connect to Pods via label selectors
slides.narration: Three objects matter most here. A Pod is the smallest deployable unit and runs your container. A Deployment manages a set of identical Pods, handling scaling, self-healing, and rolling updates — this is what you create for a stateless model API. A Service gives you a stable address that load-balances across those Pods, since Pods are ephemeral and get new IPs.

slides.title: The Deployment Manifest
bullets: replicas sets how many Pods run
selector must match Pod template labels
Pin a specific image tag, never latest
containerPort exposes the app port
slides.code:
kind: Deployment
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: model-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: model-api
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: model-api
          image: registry/model-api:1.2.0
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
slides.narration: Here's a Deployment. Replicas declares how many Pods you want. The selector tells the Deployment which Pods it owns, and it must match the labels in the Pod template — a very common bug is a mismatch here. Notice we pin a specific image tag, version one-point-two-point-zero, never latest, so rollouts and rollbacks are predictable.

slides.title: Exposing with a Service
bullets: ClusterIP: internal only (default)
NodePort: opens a port on each node, good for testing
LoadBalancer: external endpoint on cloud
port is the Service port; targetPort is the container port
slides.code:
kind: Service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: model-api
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
slides.narration: A Service selects Pods by label and routes traffic to them. ClusterIP, the default, is reachable only inside the cluster. NodePort opens a port on every node for quick testing. LoadBalancer provisions an external load balancer on cloud providers. Note that port is what clients hit on the Service, while targetPort is the port your container listens on.

slides.title: Probes & Resources
bullets: Readiness probe: only send traffic when model is loaded
Liveness probe: restart hung or deadlocked Pods
requests drive scheduling decisions
limits cap CPU and memory to prevent OOM
Critical for model APIs that load large weights
slides.code:
readinessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /ready
    port: 8080
  initialDelaySeconds: 10
resources:
  requests: { cpu: "250m", memory: "512Mi" }
  limits:   { cpu: "1",   memory: "1Gi" }
slides.narration: Probes and resources are what make a deployment production-ready. A readiness probe stops traffic from hitting a Pod that's still loading model weights. A liveness probe restarts a Pod that has hung. Resource requests influence scheduling, while limits cap usage to avoid out-of-memory kills and noisy neighbors. For memory-hungry models, getting these right is essential.

slides.title: Apply & Verify
bullets: kubectl apply -f to create/update objects
kubectl get pods / get deployment to check status
kubectl logs and describe for debugging
port-forward to test without external exposure
slides.code:
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
kubectl apply -f service.yaml
kubectl get pods -l app=model-api
kubectl logs <pod-name>
kubectl port-forward svc/model-api 8080:80
slides.narration: You apply manifests with kubectl apply. Then verify with get pods and get deployment to confirm everything is running and ready. When things go wrong, logs and describe are your first stops. And port-forward lets you hit the Service locally for a quick smoke test without exposing it to the internet.

slides.title: Scaling & Rolling Updates
bullets: kubectl scale to change replica count
kubectl set image triggers a rolling update
rollout status to watch progress
rollout undo to revert a bad release
Zero-downtime when probes are configured
slides.code:
kubectl scale deployment model-api --replicas=5
kubectl set image deployment/model-api \
  model-api=registry/model-api:1.3.0
kubectl rollout status deployment/model-api
kubectl rollout undo deployment/model-api
slides.narration: Finally, operations. Scale up or down with kubectl scale. Updating the image triggers a rolling update — new Pods come up before old ones are removed, giving zero-downtime releases when your probes are correct. Watch progress with rollout status, and if a release misbehaves, rollout undo reverts to the previous version. These commands are your everyday toolkit.

slides.title: Common Pitfalls
bullets: Selector labels not matching template labels
Using the latest tag breaks rollbacks
Missing readiness probe sends traffic too early
No resource requests causes scheduling and OOM issues
slides.narration: Before we close, watch for these recurring mistakes: selector labels that don't match the Pod template, using the latest tag which makes rollbacks unpredictable, missing readiness probes that route traffic to Pods still loading, and missing resource requests that lead to poor scheduling and out-of-memory kills. Avoid these and your deployments will be far more stable.
